articles.title: Salmon, a symbol of an industry
articles.summary: Once reserved for celebratory meals, salmon has become the most consumed fish in France in just a few decades. Behind this troubling consumption lies the story of an industry that turned salmon into a mass-market product.
articles.heroImageAlt: Salmon farming pens in a coastal bay

segments.text: The story of farmed salmon begins with an ocean that has changed beyond recognition. In a century, global fish consumption has increased ninefold, according to the
Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO)
. This transformation did not happen by chance.

After the Second World War, fishing capacity grew dramatically. Large industrial fishing fleets from countries such as France, China, and Russia set out to sea. On land, fresh-fish and canned-food markets expanded, and eating habits changed.

Frozen ready meals and aquaculture, the farming of fish, particularly salmon, grew in their wake. Industrial fish farms began in Norway in the 1960s. Gradually, the model spread to the few countries with natural conditions suited to salmon farming.

blocks.alt: Packaged salmon fillets displayed in a supermarket case
blocks.caption: Farmed salmon has become a mass-market product.

segments.text: In 2021, four countries produced 90% of the world's farmed salmon,
according to the FAO
. Norway accounted for more than half, Chile for a quarter, followed at a distance by the United Kingdom and Canada.

Among all fish, the industry established Atlantic salmon, Salmo salar, as the farmed species of choice. Several reasons explain that decision. Wild salmon was already a festive luxury at the table. Aquaculture made it widely available within a few years. For producers, it had one decisive advantage: it could be raised in large numbers in cages. In short, fish farming borrowed the methods of industrial agriculture.

blocks.alt: Fresh salmon steaks displayed on ice
blocks.caption: Salmon is often marketed for its color and boneless flesh.

segments.text: In their advertising, salmon producers promote the rosy color and boneless flesh of their fish. They also highlight their fat content and omega-3s, leaving the toxic substances in fish flesh out of view. Over time, their marketing campaigns won over the public.

Since the 1980s, farmed salmon production has grown at an extraordinary pace worldwide, and the trend shows no sign of stopping. Norway, the world's leading producer, aims to triple its annual output by 2050. To achieve this, it is betting on new, highly energy-intensive and damaging technologies: land-based and offshore farming.

blocks.alt: Salmon farming pens installed off a coastline
blocks.caption: Salmon farming is expanding from fjords to offshore facilities.

segments.text: The salmon industry is an ecological, social, and public-health time bomb. Intensive farms have disastrous consequences: greenhouse-gas emissions, animal cruelty, deforestation, worsening overfishing, and the plundering of other communities' resources, not to mention the effects on our health.

France plays a leading role in this story. It is Europe's largest salmon consumer and the world's fourth largest, making it a major player in the sector. It therefore bears particular responsibility for how these practices evolve.

The paradox is striking. Depending on the omega-3 type considered (DHA/EPA or ALA), 89% to 99% of the French population has insufficient levels. Despite high salmon consumption, the needs of most people in France are not being met.

From luxury food to intensive farming, salmon tells the story of an industry that has reshaped our eating habits. But its nutritional promises do not hold up against the figures. This calls for us to stop overconsuming farmed salmon, and highlights the urgent need to transform our food system.
To learn more about the inner workings and harms of the salmon industry, read our report:
Salmon: the pink bomb of a food system running out of steam

articles.title: How can we replace fish on our plates?
articles.summary: An interview with Marie Laforêt, a leading voice in plant-based cooking
articles.heroImageAlt: Marie Laforêt, author of Seafood Vegan

segments.text: Where should you start? What can you cook when you want a dish with a taste of the sea? To answer these questions, Marie Laforêt published Seafood Vegan with Solar, a recipe book that is as beautiful as it is informative. She spoke with Seastemik about it.

blocks.text: Marie, you are a leading figure in plant-based cooking in France. You have published more than 20 recipe books in 15 years. Why did you decide to focus on the world of the sea this time?

segments.text: Marie Laforêt: Among all the vegan cookbooks published in France, many explain how to replace land animals in our diets, but very few offer alternatives to marine animals. Also, people who decide to eat less meat, or stop eating it altogether, often turn to fish. That was true for me when I was younger! I think this is a real problem, especially since we often forget that far more marine animals are killed for food than land animals. For all these reasons, it was important to me to write a book devoted to this subject. It is a project I have been working on for a long time. Several of my books already include sections devoted entirely to it, but I felt it deserved a book of its own.

blocks.text: You mentioned that you used to eat fish. How much were marine animals part of your diet? When and why did you stop eating them?

segments.text: Marie Laforêt: I grew up in a Breton family where marine animals were regularly served at the table, especially during the holiday season. As a teenager, and later when I stopped eating land animals, I started eating even more fish, particularly salmon! Then, in 2008, I realized that fish were sentient beings too. From an ethical point of view, it did not make sense to me to eat some animals but not others. That year, I became vegetarian.

blocks.text: What would you say to someone questioning their diet and thinking about eating less fish or stopping altogether?

segments.text: Marie Laforêt: I would start by saying that it is important to question what we put on our plates. We do not all eat fish for the same reasons. Sometimes it is habit. Sometimes it is pleasure. Sometimes it is because we believe fish is essential to good health. The ways to cut down or stop will differ depending on what motivates us.

blocks.text: Could you talk us through those different approaches?

segments.text: Marie Laforêt: If you eat fish for protein, you can simply choose a plant-based source of protein, in whatever flavor or form you like. If you eat fish for omega-3s, oils, nuts and seeds, and supplements can meet your needs. And if it is about taste, plant-based recipes like the ones in my book will do the trick. For example, if you want to keep a family recipe made with fish and passed down through generations, such as bouillabaisse, you can absolutely create a plant-based version. Giving up fish does not mean abandoning our traditions, but letting them evolve. And if you need inspiration, my book is there for you.

blocks.alt: A plant-based recipe inspired by seafood
blocks.caption: Seafood Vegan offers plant-based alternatives to seafood dishes.

blocks.text: Who is your new book, Seafood Vegan, for? Is it accessible to people who do not cook much, or is it aimed at experienced plant-based cooks?

segments.text: Marie Laforêt: I really wrote this book for everyone. It includes very simple recipes with easy-to-find ingredients. I also chose to include more creative and technical recipes for people who enjoy trying new dishes, making convincing alternatives, or creating plant-based versions of family favorites. Some of the recipes I created for this book are alternatives to dishes I had not eaten for 15 years!

blocks.text: To create convincing alternatives, you researched how marine animals are prepared and cooked. How did you go about it?

segments.text: Marie Laforêt: I did a great deal of research into these processes, especially for salmon. You might think smoked salmon, gravlax, and nova lox are the same thing, but they are not. Gravlax is salmon cured in salt. As its name suggests, smoked salmon is smoked over beechwood rather than cured. Nova lox falls between the two: it is both cured and smoked. This research helped me develop precise plant-based recipes with subtle flavors and textures.

blocks.text: Beyond this technical research, what inspired the book?

segments.text: Marie Laforêt: I drew inspiration from French classics, of course, such as bouillabaisse, sole meunière, and moules marinières, as well as my family recipes. I also looked to recipes from many other countries, coastal specialties, and street food. One cuisine particularly inspired me: the Japanese techniques of imitation known as modoki ryōri, rooted in Buddhist traditions. People may think that imitating the flesh of land or marine animals is a recent idea from Western vegans. In fact, vegan eating has been a tradition for hundreds or even thousands of years in some Asian countries.

blocks.alt: Marie Laforêt with her plant-based cookbook
blocks.caption: Marie Laforêt draws on a range of culinary traditions for her recipes.

blocks.text: Your book includes several plant-based alternatives to salmon. Which would you recommend to someone who has never cooked one?

segments.text: Marie Laforêt: I would suggest starting with a recipe where the animal flesh is not raw, so not an alternative to a salmon fillet. Salmon-style rillettes are among my favorite recipes, and they are easy to make. I make them myself every Christmas, and my family always loves them. The recipe is truly impressive in its color, texture, and flavor.

blocks.text: Plant-based alternatives to salmon, such as smoked salmon substitutes, are sometimes available in shops. Have you tried any? What did you think?

segments.text: Marie Laforêt: One Christmas, I bought a smoked salmon alternative and felt as if I were eating a kind of sausage rather than smoked salmon! I was really disappointed, but I understood then that smoky flavor is not just one thing: there are several very different kinds. I talk about this in my book. A successful smoked salmon alternative uses a beechwood-smoked condiment, the wood traditionally used to smoke salmon.

blocks.text: Anything else you would like to share?

segments.text: Marie Laforêt: Yes. If you are hesitating to reduce or stop eating marine animals, I know that your loved ones' potential reactions can hold you back. In my view, the best thing to do is cook delicious recipes for them. Sometimes a delicious dish is worth more than a thousand words. Plant-based tarama, for example, is just as good as, or even better than, the cheap industrial version. Recipe by recipe, it is easier to convince people through taste than through ideas or arguments. Some of my recipes have become holiday classics in my family, even though I can tell you it was not a sure thing at first!

articles.title: SALMO, the incredible story of a wild salmon
articles.summary: A river, a forest, an estuary, the ocean, and then glaciers. Salmon spend their lives connecting worlds we think of as separate. Selected for many festivals, the animated short film SALMO tells the incredible journey of wild salmon and shows how fragile the ecosystems they cross are.
articles.heroImageAlt: Artwork from the animated short film SALMO

segments.text: It is the story of a wild salmon leaving its home river to reach the ocean. In SALMO, we follow a young salmon on a journey spanning thousands of kilometers: eight minutes of poetry and adventurous twists. Eight minutes, too, in which we confront a sobering reality: Atlantic salmon populations are in alarming decline, and the ecosystems they travel through are being severely degraded by human activity.
Directed by Paul Pajot and produced by La Méridienne, the short invites us to pause our human perspective. We experience everything from a salmon’s point of view.

This deliberate perspective reveals, among other things, the invisible connections between the different environments salmon pass through during their lives. Contrary to what we might think, these spaces are far from isolated.

blocks.alt: A scene from the animated short film SALMO
blocks.caption: SALMO reveals ecosystems from a salmon’s point of view.

blocks.text: A journey seen through salmon’s eyes

segments.text: This film is not only the story of a salmon. It is also the story of a living world that we are part of. The animation’s vivid painting creates a sense of symbiosis and reveals the ecological continuity between river, estuary, and ocean.

SALMO lets us see biological phenomena that are invisible to the naked eye and often little known, such as smoltification. During their journey, salmon move from fresh water to salt water. To adapt, their gills change so they can expel salt.

blocks.alt: A scene from the salmon’s journey in SALMO
blocks.caption: The film follows the different stages of a salmon’s journey.

segments.text: In this short film, Paul Pajot chose to bring a sensitive dimension to serious issues. He drew on extensive scientific research to write it. Through this thoughtful approach, he helps us understand that protecting salmon is not only about protecting a species: it is also about protecting the environments all life depends on, including us.

blocks.text: Connecting with the living world, one story at a time

segments.text: Born during the 2020 lockdown, SALMO became a collective adventure bringing together artists, animators, musicians, and salmon specialists. The film has since been selected for around twenty festivals and continues to be shown both as a work of art and as an educational tool.

This sensitive way of telling stories about ecological issues is part of a broader movement supported by Seastemik. Connecting with the living world, one story at a time, helps us learn about our environment and care for the world we move through.

articles.title: 5 misconceptions about fish (and why they are false)
articles.summary: Being as silent as a carp, cursing someone with a fishy insult, or having a goldfish memory… These expressions reveal how little we value and know about fish. Let’s take a closer look at common misconceptions and learn to see these marine animals differently.
articles.heroImageAlt: Illustration of fish for the article about common misconceptions

segments.text: From childhood, we build our relationship with the living world. Shaped by scientific, cultural, and religious histories, this process tends to distinguish species and rank them, wherever we live.

In Europe, for example, we learn early to distinguish animals we love, such as kittens, from animals we eat, such as salmon. In other words, we treat some animals as individuals and others as resources. Fish on our plates are clearly among the animals we respect the least.

Yet fish, like us and like kittens, are sentient beings. They have a subjective experience of the world: they can perceive their surroundings, learn, remember, and feel pleasure, fear, and pain. Fish are living beings, and challenging certain clichés can help us recognize them as such.

blocks.alt: Illustration accompanying the section about fish memory

segments.text: Marine animals’ abilities have long been underestimated. The claim that fish have a “three-second memory” is one of the first myths to challenge. Fish can learn from experience and remember it long enough to change their behavior.

For example, they can recognize their environment, remember where to find food, avoid dangerous areas, or associate certain signals with a reward or a threat. In some species, memory also plays a role in navigation and social interactions.

blocks.alt: Illustration accompanying the section about fish sensitivity

segments.text: A fish’s inability to cry out does not mean it cannot suffer. Like us, fish have a nervous system. They can detect stimuli that may harm their bodies, such as extreme heat.
Studies show that fish change their behavior and physiological responses when faced with potentially painful situations.
We cannot ask fish to tell us what they feel (though we might like to), but they really do experience pleasure, fear, stress, and pain.

blocks.alt: Illustration accompanying the section about fish communication

segments.text: It is easy to imagine fish living in a silent world without interaction. Yet fish do communicate. Their language and signals are simply different from ours.

Depending on the species, they use visual, chemical, acoustic, or physical signals to share information with one another. Some species live in structured societies with complex interactions. In short, an animal does not have to resemble us to have a social life.

blocks.alt: Illustration accompanying the section about fish consumption

segments.text: We say “a dog,” “a cat,” or “an elephant,” but talk about “salmon,” “tuna,” or “trout.” Our own language makes invisible the sensitivity and intelligence of the marine animals we eat. Describing them in kilos, portions, and fillets helps rationalize their exploitation and ease our consciences.
But a salmon is not a fillet. A trout is not a portion. A fish is not a product. Before it became “salmon” on a plate, that salmon was a living, sentient animal.

blocks.alt: Illustration accompanying the section about fishing and fish farming

segments.text: The image of a lone fisher with a line and a small boat has fueled the idea that eating fish is an ancient, even “natural,” practice. Yet, depending on the era and region, our diets have most often been plant-based.

This image of a lone fisher is far removed from today’s food system. Fish sold in shops are either caught by gigantic trawlers that sweep the seabed for miles or intensively farmed in marine and even land-based facilities. This is not small-scale fishing; it is an industry.

One logic drives this industry: produce more, faster, and at lower cost to supply a global market. Fish become volumes, tons, yields, and margins. Even aquaculture’s vocabulary says a lot: “biomass,” “growth,” “feed conversion ratio,” and “yield.” But a ton of fish is not a ton of biomass; it is countless individual animals.
Salmon are surprising living beings. Learning more about their bodies and lives helps us see that they, like us, are sentient animals. Discover five things you probably do not know about salmon.
